sections.html:
Farmington is in east-central Davis County and is the county seat. It covers about 10 square miles at an elevation of 4,246 feet, with Kaysville and Fruit Heights to the north, Centerville to the south, the Wasatch Mountains to the east and the Great Salt Lake to the west.

The city describes itself as sitting between Ogden and Salt Lake City, roughly a half-hour commute from job centers in both.

sections.h2: What is the history of Farmington?
sections.html:
Hector C. Haight wintered cattle in Farmington's grassy lowlands in 1847 and 1848, and five other families soon joined him. In 1852 the territorial legislature created Davis County and made the settlement, then called North Cottonwood, its county seat, renaming it Farmington.

Residents built Utah's first courthouse in 1854 and 1855, a two-story adobe building, and partly walled the town with mud. The Utah Central Railroad arrived in 1870, and the city incorporated on December 15, 1892 with 1,180 residents. Simon Bamberger developed the Lagoon resort in 1896, and it grew into Utah's largest amusement park.

The 2020 census counted 24,531 people, up from 18,275 in 2010. In 1990 the population was close to 10,000, so the city has more than doubled in about three decades.

sections.h2: What does the economy of Farmington look like?
sections.html:
Farmington combines county government with retail and tourism draws. As the county seat, it hosts Davis County offices, including Tax Administration at 61 South Main Street.

  • Lagoon Amusement Park occupies about 100 acres in the city.
  • Station Park is a transit-oriented shopping center that includes a FrontRunner station.
  • The S&S Shortline Railroad Park and Museum displays more than 90 pieces of railroad equipment.
  • A commercial center along Highway 89 developed in the late 1980s.

The city says most large businesses sit on its outskirts, which keeps traffic out of the older central area. The Clark Lane Historic District, built around houses from early settler Ezra T. Clark, is on the National Register of Historic Places.

sections.h2: How do weather and flooding affect Farmington houses?
sections.html:
Farmington has real winters. Average annual snowfall is 48.6 inches and average precipitation is 22.25 inches, with a July average high of 92.5 degrees and a January average low of 20.6. Lake-enhanced snow can arrive in the cold months.

The state's history page also records flash floods in the town in the 1920s and 1930s and again in 1984. The Farmington Area Pressurized Irrigation District began serving homeowners and remaining farmers in July 1978, so ask whether your lot is on that system.

  • Ask your insurance agent whether a flood policy applies to a parcel near a creek or canyon mouth.
  • Keep the roof age and any snow or water damage repairs on paper.
  • Note whether the yard uses pressurized irrigation, since buyers may ask.

sections.h2: Which schools and trails serve Farmington?
sections.html:
Farmington schools belong to the Davis School District, and the city also lists charter and private options nearby. Outdoor access is a draw: the Farmington Trail Committee maintains 146.49 miles of trails, including 36 named trails and 55 points of interest. The city also holds Farmington Festival Days each year.

Hiking, biking and horseback riding in the canyons and foothills are part of how the city markets itself, and wetlands and orchards are within reach. If you are selling a house near a trailhead, mention that access in any conversation with a buyer.

sections.h2: What are Farmington's rules for accessory dwelling units?
sections.html:
Farmington allows two kinds of accessory units and a third option that lets an owner split a detached unit onto its own lot. Only one ADU is allowed per single-family home.

  • Internal ADU: inside or attached to the main home, on a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
  • Detached ADU: a permanent structure on a foundation, on a lot of at least 10,000 square feet.
  • Subordinate single-family dwelling: a separate lot with its own home, subject to subdivision approval.

Either the main home or the ADU must be owner-occupied. A subordinate dwelling must be owner-occupied for two years after ownership is separated from the main home. Each unit needs its own full kitchen and bathroom and one off-street parking space beyond the main home's parking, and rentals must run 30 days or longer, so an ADU cannot be a short-term rental.

Converting space for an internal ADU requires a building permit unless the space was already approved for residential occupancy. A basement unit with no paperwork can complicate any sale that depends on a mortgage.

sections.h2: How do property taxes and appeals work in Farmington?
sections.html:
Farmington parcels are billed by Davis County, and Utah's state calendar sets the main dates. Taxes are due November 30, and the 45% primary residential exemption means a primary home is taxed on 55% of its market value.

The Davis County Controller mails the Notice of Assessors' Property Market Valuation at the end of July. If you disagree with the value, you can appeal to the Board of Equalization, which is the Davis County Commission. The county page gives the deadline as September 16 in one place and September 15, 2026 in another, so confirm the date with Tax Administration at 801-451-3331 before filing.

Only the market value can be appealed, not the tax rate, and only the owner or an agent with a notarized authorization may file. Accepted evidence includes:

  • closing documents signed by the title agent,
  • a full appraisal by a certified appraiser,
  • sales of at least three comparable properties near January 1,
  • documented factual errors, such as the wrong square footage.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work in Farmington?
sections.html:
A cash sale in Farmington has fewer moving parts than a financed one because no lender reviews the house. You tell us about the property, we look at it and nearby sales, and you decide whether to accept the offer.

  1. Share the address and basic details.
  2. We review the house and the neighborhood.
  3. You accept or decline.
  4. A title company runs the title search and sets the closing date.
  5. The deed is recorded and you are paid at closing.

If the tax bill is unpaid or an ADU never got its permit, tell the title company early so those items can be resolved before the deed is recorded.

sections.h2: What do Farmington sellers commonly face?
sections.html:
A few issues are worth checking before you sell a Farmington house.

  • An older house in or near the historic district that needs updating.
  • A basement apartment that was never permitted as an internal ADU.
  • A detached unit that the owner wants to sell separately, which the city treats as a subordinate single-family dwelling needing subdivision approval.
  • A valuation notice the owner disagrees with and wants to appeal before selling.

Each of these can slow a traditional listing. A direct sale lets you skip staging and repair work and move on the timeline you choose.

faqs.q: What county is Farmington, Utah in?
faqs.a: Davis County. Farmington is the county seat, and the county's Tax Administration office is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Farmington?
faqs.a: November 30, the statewide due date. Taxes unpaid after that date become delinquent, with a reduced penalty if everything is paid by January 31.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Farmington property value?
faqs.a: File with the Davis County Board of Equalization after the valuation notice arrives at the end of July. The county page lists September 15 or 16 as the deadline, so confirm with Tax Administration. You can appeal only the market value.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a Farmington ADU for short stays?
faqs.a: No. Farmington requires ADU rentals to be 30 days or longer, and the owner must live in either the main home or the ADU.

faqs.q: What size lot do I need for a detached ADU in Farmington?
faqs.a: At least 10,000 square feet. An internal ADU needs a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
